title: Your breath routine
hook: assemble three minutes from this week, your way

segments.voice: Yesterday we carried a plain word on the breath. Your line was here. Did you catch yourself three steps ahead, and come back to here? Day one hundred three.

Think of a kitchen after a week of cooking lessons. Monday you learned to chop. Tuesday, a sauce. Wednesday, how not to burn rice. Nobody expects you to cook every dish every night. What you want by Sunday is one meal you can make without the book, the one you'll actually cook on a tired Thursday. This week was a cooking class for the breath. Six ways in. Today there's nothing new to learn. Today you put three minutes together, from what fits you, and make it yours. Today: your breath routine.
screen: `A WEEK OF COOKING LESSONS.` → `ONE MEAL WITHOUT THE BOOK.` → `THREE MINUTES THAT FIT YOU.`

segments.voice: Let's lay the week out on the counter. Day one: just watching. Letting it breathe, without fixing anything. Your line was it breathes. Day two: longer out than in, four in, six out, the slow exhale that tends to calm the body. Day three: the double sigh, two inhales and one long exhale, the body's own reset, from the small Stanford study. Day four: counting to ten, and starting again at one without drama. Day five: box breathing, four equal sides, a job for a racing mind. Day six: breath with a word, and our plain word, here. Six tools. Different jobs. Watching is for knowing where you are. The long exhale is for winding down. The sigh is for a quick reset. Counting trains the noticing. The box keeps your head in a hard moment. The word gives the mind a handrail. Here's a simple way to build three minutes. Start with a minute of just watching, so you know what today's breath is like before you change it. Then a minute of one tool, whichever the day needs: long exhales if you're wound up, counting if you're scattered, a few sighs if you're heavy. Then a last minute of breath with the word, here, to land. That's one shape. It isn't the only one. The point of this week is that it's yours now. A routine you like is one you'll keep, and a practice you keep matters more than a perfect one you drop.
screen: `SIX TOOLS, SIX JOBS.` · `A MINUTE TO WATCH.` · `A MINUTE FOR WHAT TODAY NEEDS.` · `A MINUTE TO LAND.` · then, large: `THREE MINUTES, YOURS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: your three minutes. First, just watch the breath for a few rounds, the way we did on day one. Ask: what does today need? Wound up, scattered, heavy, or steady? Then choose one tool and use it: long exhales, a few double sighs, counting to ten, or a couple of boxes. Then finish with the word: here on the in-breath, here on the out-breath. If a different order suits you, use it. The bell holds the time.
Your breath routine. Three minutes built from this week's six tools, in the shape that fits you. Today's word.

Your line: three minutes, yours. Today, pick a time you already have, after coffee, before the car, before sleep, and do your three minutes there. Tomorrow a new week begins: mornings and evenings. Day one hundred three.

howItsDone: People who keep a breathing practice often settle on a short routine of their own: a minute of watching, a minute of one technique, and a minute to settle, done at the same time each day.

original.note: Greek: training, exercise, the way an athlete trains. Ancient philosophers used it for daily practice of the mind. It gives English the word ascetic.

trapdoor: what you thought: a routine is a set of rules to follow.
what it means: a short practice you build from what fits you, so you'll actually keep it.
what a scholar hears: askēsis, training, the Greek word philosophers used for daily exercises of the mind, the way athletes trained the body.
